extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers seeking an encyclopedic overview of the novel American Dirt, its reception, and controversy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the evaluative criteria and standards critics, reviewers, and industry actors used when judging or promoting the novel American Dirt — e.g., authenticity, prose, characterization, marketing ethics, and industry representation. Useful for assessing how a contemporary novel is critiqued on cultural and literary grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural authenticity / credible depiction of culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the book credibly represents Mexican culture and lived realities of Mexican people; critics described the book as 'culturally exploitative' and questioned Lydia's credibility as a Mexican.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics argued that a believable portrayal requires knowledge and credible internal perspective of the community depicted; anti-patterns include portraying a character as surprised by commonplace realities ('so shocked by her own country’s day-to-day realities') which undermines authenticity. The page records accusations the book 'reeks of opportunism' and is 'appropriating' when it flattens or misrepresents the culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial positionality and identity relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of whether the author's background and ties to the subject matter affect the legitimacy of writing on that topic; the book was criticized partly because the author was a European-born woman in the U.S. 'without ties to the Mexican migrant experience.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors consider whether the author has the lived experience, perspective, or sufficient research to responsibly tell the story; absence of ties can intensify criticism about appropriation and inauthenticity. Conversely, defenders argue a talented writer can create convincing works about other cultures if the 'hard work' is done.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and research into subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the novel is 'accurate' and 'well-informed' about the migrant experience; negative descriptions include 'inaccurate' and 'ill-informed'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion assesses factual plausibility and respect for the real-world phenomena depicted (e.g., migration routes, dangers). Anti-patterns: oversimplification, factual errors, or portrayals that feel stereotyped or sensationalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation and impact on marginalized writers/communities
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether publication and promotion of the book harms or sidelines marginalized authors; the controversy sparked the #DignidadLiteraria campaign demanding greater Latino representation and an investigation into discriminatory practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics evaluate not only the text but its industry effects: does it take opportunities, advance payouts, or attention away from writers from the represented community? Positive actions include publisher commitments to boost representation; negative outcomes include perceived silencing or displacement of authentic voices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prose quality and stylistic execution
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal assessment of writing craft; The New York Times reviewer Parul Sehgal said the book had 'stilted prose and characterizations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators look at sentence-level style, voice, imagery, and whether prose serves narrative goals. 'Stilted' prose and awkward metaphors/phrasing are cited as faults. Positive assessments emphasize moving, vivid writing that brings readers into characters' experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization and psychological credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether characters are believable, fully formed, and psychologically credible; critics accused the novel of weak characterization and constructing characters to serve plot or sentiment ('substituting characters arc for mere trauma').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good characterization shows internal consistency, believable reactions, and depth; anti-patterns include flat characters, manipulative arcs, or characters presented mainly as vessels for trauma rather than as nuanced people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of trauma and emotional manipulation (trauma-porn)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the novel responsibly depicts suffering or lapses into 'trauma-porn melodrama'; some reviewers called it 'harmful, appropriating, inaccurate, trauma-porn melodrama.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess if traumatic events are depicted with nuance and respect rather than sensationalized for shock or easy sympathy. Warning signs include overuse of sensational suffering to elicit emotion without context or complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative perspective and who the story centers
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the novel centers the appropriate viewpoint and how that affects reader sympathy; critics argued the book's construction 'makes it easier for sheltered, white American readers to sympathize with the plot.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whose perspectives are prioritized and whether that centering simplifies or reshapes the real dynamics of the subject. A critique can be that an outsider-oriented perspective domesticates complex social realities for outside readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketing ethics and sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether promotional tactics and marketing decisions are appropriate and sensitive to subject matter; Flatiron's use of 'barbed wire decorations' at launch and other publicity steps were criticized as clumsy or tasteless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers should align promotional choices with ethical considerations of the book's themes and subjects. Anti-patterns: gimmicks that appear to exploit trauma or reinforce harmful imagery; responsive action includes public apologies and changes to campaign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry endorsement and blurbing practices
rubrics_metrics.description: How endorsements, blurbs, and high-profile picks (e.g., Oprah's Book Club) influence reception and whether such platforms should reconsider selections when concerns arise; Oprah's endorsement drew substantial pushback and calls for rescinding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators may weigh the responsibility of influential endorsers to vet works for representational harm. The use of prominent blurbs can amplify both praise and criticism; controversies can prompt open letters and public debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success versus critical legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tension between bestseller status and literary or ethical judgment: American Dirt was a #1 New York Times bestseller and sold millions despite intense criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sales and awards are separate metrics from ethical and artistic appraisal. A work's commercial popularity may not resolve debates about authenticity or merit; evaluators often note both metrics when assessing impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsiveness to criticism and publisher accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: How authors and publishers respond to public criticism and demands (e.g., Flatiron agreed to boost Latinx representation after backlash; tour cancellations and statements acknowledging marketing missteps).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-publication actions — apologies, policy changes, engagement with marginalized communities — factor into judgments about institutional responsibility. Failure to respond appropriately can exacerbate reputational harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety and logistical considerations in promotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions about author events and tours in light of threats and public backlash (Flatiron cancelled the tour 'citing threats to Cummins').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not a literary quality, organizers must balance promotion with safety; this criterion looks at prudent event planning and responses to credible threats or controversy.
